title: Lagaan Turns 25. The Team Just Reunited, and They're Making Another Cricket Epic.
excerpt: A Spotify reunion, a three-day theatrical re-release, and a new Aamir-Ashutosh biopic on Lala Amarnath — the Lagaan universe just got its second innings.
body:
It started, as the best things do, with a memory no one asked for but everyone needed.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=nOOoVLu1kak</youtube>

On a stage in Mumbai last week, **Aamir Khan**, **A.R. Rahman**, **Javed Akhtar**, and **Ashutosh Gowariker** sat down together for Spotify's first-ever live recording of *Behind the Beats* — and for ninety minutes, four men who changed Indian cinema talked about it like they still couldn't believe it happened.

Rahman recalled the initial skepticism. A period cricket film set in 1893? With songs in languages most Bollywood audiences had never heard in a commercial movie? Akhtar admitted he had reservations about the scale. And Gowariker, who spent years developing the screenplay, described the shoot in Bhuj as the most physically demanding experience of his career — 120 days in scorching Kutch, with a crew that included real villagers who'd never seen a camera.

**Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India** was released on June 15, 2001. It was the most expensive Indian film of its time. It became the third Indian film to be nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. And 25 years later, it returned to theaters on June 12, 13, and 14 — a limited re-release that sold out shows in multiple cities.

> "A timeless epic that touched every heart. On the 25th Anniversary of LAGAAN, the epic saga returns to the big screen." — Aamir Khan Productions

## Why It Still Hits

For the Indian diaspora, Lagaan was never just a movie. It was the film you took your non-Indian friends to. The one that made cricket legible to Americans. The one whose soundtrack — *Ghanan Ghanan*, *Mitwa*, *Radha Kaise Na Jale*, *O Rey Chhori* — became the default playlist for every desi house party, Navratri night, and road trip from Jersey to Jackson Heights.

The underdog narrative — villagers who learn cricket from scratch to defeat their colonial rulers — landed differently abroad. For NRIs navigating their own version of proving themselves in someone else's country, **Bhuvan's defiance wasn't historical fiction. It was personal.**

At the Spotify event, Rahman played fragments of *Chale Chalo* and the room collectively lost it. Javed Akhtar explained the logic behind embedding Awadhi and Braj dialect lyrics into a mainstream film — something that would be considered suicidal for commercial viability by today's Bollywood standards. Gowariker described how the cricket sequences were choreographed like action set pieces, with six cameras running simultaneously.

## The Reunion No One Expected

But the real headline came from offstage. According to a Pinkvilla report, **Aamir Khan and Ashutosh Gowariker are reuniting for a new period cricket biopic** — this time based on the life of **Lala Amarnath**, the first Indian batter to score a Test century for India. The film, set against the backdrop of the India-Pakistan Partition, is reportedly in advanced scripting stages, with **Rajkumar Hirani** and **Abhijat Joshi** contributing creatively to the screenplay.

Shooting is expected to begin around September 2026, making it one of Aamir's biggest commitments in years. The man who gave us Lagaan is going back to cricket — only this time, the story is real.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

Lagaan's re-release in India coincides with the FIFA World Cup dominating screens globally, which makes the timing both poetic and strategic. Cricket and national pride, once again, competing with the world's biggest sporting stage.

For those in the US, UK, and Canada hoping for international screenings, no formal announcement has been made yet — but the Spotify event and the flood of social media nostalgia suggest demand is more than there. If the Dhurandhar 2 theatrical re-release could pull ₹32 crore in its re-run, Lagaan in 4K with Rahman's remastered score would be an event.

Twenty-five years later, the film that proved India could make a global epic on its own terms is back. And the men who made it are getting the band back together.

Some stories don't age. They just wait for the right innings.
